s7-e11-from-chaos-monkey-for-spring-boot-to-a-138m-automated-reliability-engine-with-benjamin-wilms-of-steadybit

Open Source Sparked the Company: Wilms built Chaos Monkey for Spring Boot to test a system before its first production release. Its adoption led Instana co-founder Mirko Novakovic to give him money to start a company.

An Agent-Based MVP: With only six to eight months of money in the bank, the team built an MVP where users install an agent once, then focus on their use case instead of mastering many separate chaos tools.
Good Enough for Now: Once a feature delivers value and gives someone an aha moment, Steadybit's approach is to stop, gather feedback, and then iterate rather than chase perfection.
Founders Do the Job First: Wilms would not hire a VP of sales before selling the product himself. He also warns that growing a team too fast strains runway and destroys culture.
Incorporation Order Matters: Looking back, Wilms would create a Delaware company first and then a German one. Starting as a German company meant a tax issue blocked a later flip to the States.

q: Why did Benjamin Wilms create Chaos Monkey for Spring Boot?
a: Working as a consultant, Benjamin Wilms could not gain confidence in a system headed to production just by looking at its code and tests, and existing chaos tools were not a good fit. As he put it, "I need to do it in a different way because I'm a developer." [03:46]

q: What was the first version of Steadybit like?
a: Benjamin Wilms describes an MVP built around installing an agent once, so users did not have to become experts in many different tools. After that, he said, "at that point in time, you can focus on your use case." [06:13]

q: How does Steadybit decide what to build next?
a: Benjamin Wilms balances feedback from early users with a long-term vision that the company validates with customers. Rather than asking customers to name the next feature, he focuses on their problems, because a customer is "more able to describe a specific problem" [08:37].

q: What is Benjamin Wilms' advice on startup hiring?
a: Benjamin Wilms advises hiring motivated, product-focused people, starting with those you already know, and not scaling the team too fast or too early. He also believes founders should learn a job before hiring an expert for it: "I will not hire and let's say VP of sales before I was not able to sell my" [13:00] product.

q: How has Steadybit evolved beyond chaos engineering?
a: Benjamin Wilms says the product is moving toward an orchestration platform that integrates with load testing, monitoring, APM and observability tools. Customers helped the team see chaos engineering differently, to "call it more like an engine, something you will use." [16:44]

Docs Are a Constant Need: Fedora project leader Matthew Miller says there are always new things to explain. Few people are strong at both writing and programming or system administration, and insiders can miss what outsiders need explained.

Documentation as a Technical On-Ramp: Ben Cotton began in Fedora docs able to barely code and is now a Fedora program manager. The work taught him the software, Git, scripting and workflow automation, and made him popular with core contributors.

Scope Your First Contribution: Cotton volunteered to update the book-length RPM guide and found that, past the first few chapters, its technical depth was far beyond what he knew. Pace yourself when taking on docs work.

Write for Skimmers and Translators: Technical writer Nicole Barada advises against giant blocks of text. Start from basics like installation, expect readers of all skill levels and fields, and make the docs easy to translate.

Stale Docs Lose Users: Robin Bergeron warns that outdated or missing information confuses people and wastes the moment when they are actively engaged. Some users may persist, while others give up and move on.

q: Why do open source projects need technical documentation writers?
a: Fedora project leader Matthew Miller explains that documentation is a persistent need because projects keep changing. In Miller's words, "There's a constant need to keep up with things, and there's always new things to explain." [05:16]

q: Can writing documentation help you become more technical?
a: Yes, according to Ben Cotton, who started in Fedora documentation, learned more about the software and tools like Git, and became a Fedora program manager. Cotton also says that stepping up on docs "makes you very popular with the core contributors." [12:00]

q: Why is it hard for developers to document their own software?
a: Matthew Miller says writing and programming are very different skill sets, and being good at both is not automatic. Creators can also overlook things that seem obvious to them, as Miller notes: "Sometimes when you're the person doing something, it's hard to know exactly what to document." [09:01]

q: How should you start writing good technical documentation?
a: Nicole Barada advises writing the way you would want to read, keeping in mind that people skim and come with varied skill levels. Barada cautions, "So don't jump into a project and start writing giant blocks of text." [19:28]

q: How does documentation help end users understand a product?
a: Good documentation turns technical language into something that shows users how a product helps them. Robin Bergeron described the role as "almost being like the translator from engineering speak to human speak." [22:17]

Debt as a Byproduct: Engineering manager Tremaine Darby argues technical debt isn't necessarily bad or proof someone did something wrong. It comes from moving fast and shipping work that isn't yet the whole picture.
Sharpen the Saw: Darby likens maintenance to a tree cutter slowing down to sharpen the saw. That upkeep is what makes it possible to keep delivering well over the long term.

Documentation Drifts Immediately: Darby says a document is almost out of date as soon as it's published. Any bug fix, enhancement or other change it doesn't reflect pulls it further from the as-built software.
Inevitable in AI Work: Sherard Griffin, Red Hat's director of AI services, says AI and machine learning change so rapidly that a huge chunk of the code base will inevitably carry technical debt.

A Debt-Free World Stalls: The Compiler team doubts a world without technical debt could or should exist. Work could stay stuck in development, deadlines slip and customer needs go unmet, so the job is balancing innovation with maintenance.

q: Is technical debt always a bad thing?
a: Not according to Tremaine Darby, an engineering manager, who sees it as a result of moving fast to get things out. Darby said the negative framing is off because "it's not necessarily bad or it didn't come to be because of someone doing something wrong" [06:39].

q: Why does maintenance matter when there is pressure to ship new features?
a: Tremaine Darby compares it to cutting trees, where you sometimes have to slow down and sharpen your saw. Darby said, "So it's all those things that make it better to deliver in the long term." [07:08]

q: Why is documentation a source of technical debt?
a: Tremaine Darby explains that documentation diverges from the software whenever a bug fix, enhancement or other change isn't reflected in it. As Darby put it, "it's almost out of date as soon as you put it out" [10:59].

q: Do AI and machine learning projects accumulate technical debt?
a: Sherard Griffin, director of AI services at Red Hat, says they do, because teams on the bleeding edge don't have all the answers about how technology fits together. Griffin said of AI and machine learning, "it's such a rapidly changing environment" [13:26].

q: How do teams weigh technical debt against deadlines?
a: Sherard Griffin describes measuring the debt's effect on the team's ability to get code out the door. Griffin said the question is "how much is the technical debt impacting our ability to hit that timeline" [14:36].

The Lori Krebs Ratio: Red Hat CFO Lori Krebs puts her time at about 80% managing and leading her team and 20% on technical finance and tax work. The Compiler team names that 80/20 split after her.

Resist the Quick Fix: Director Chris Bredesen calls jumping in to fix problems seductive muscle memory that leaders should probably avoid. VP Mark Little instead helps his team see better alternatives and evolve the code without making them feel bad.

Find a Non-Blocking Outlet: Mark Little codes on holiday through projects like Advent of Code. Manager Shoshana Collins takes on small SQL queries, data pulls and mini models that keep her off the critical path.

When 90% Coding Works: Bob McWhorter codes about 90% of the time on a flat team of six senior engineers. He says other managers couldn't copy it, and that deadlines and outside dependencies make managerial duties far more important.

What Managers Gain: Moving into management means giving up much of the hands-on work, but managers described gaining influence, the ability to help others and a larger effect on company direction. The hosts also argue that returning to an individual role isn't failure.

q: How much time should a manager spend coding versus managing?
a: The episode highlights an 80/20 split of management to technical work, which the Compiler team calls the Lori Krebs ratio. Describing her own finance role, Krebs said, "I still stay in that technical mindset, but it's 80% that I spend on" [07:11] being a manager and leading the team.

q: Why can it be a problem when managers jump in to fix technical issues?
a: Chris Bredesen, a director of software engineering at Red Hat, says the muscle memory of jumping in to fix a problem is very seductive. In his view, it "is something that I think is probably not a great behavior for leaders to do." [05:54]

q: How can a manager keep technical skills sharp without blocking the team?
a: Shoshana Collins takes on small projects each week, such as SQL queries and data pulls, that stay off the critical path of major deliverables. She described them as including "little mini models or analyses that I can do that won't block my team." [19:30]

q: Why do some engineers leave management and go back to coding?
a: Bob McWhorter's first management stint lasted about 18 months and involved spreadsheets, meetings and email while others did the engineering. McWhorter recalled, "I was envious of the engineers getting to engineer while I did not." [14:19]

q: How much hands-on technical work does a Red Hat analytics manager still do?
a: Shoshana Collins follows roughly the 80/20 split and says she is not ready to close the door on being a builder. As Collins put it, "I spend about 20% of my time now actually using the skills that brought me to Red Hat." [18:57]

q: Why did Noah Labhart leave corporate IT to become an entrepreneur?

Labor Pools Buffer Shortages: Pockets of unfilled work correlated with stimulus or unemployment payments. Veryable coaches businesses to build a pool of favorite, highly rated operators they can post to directly.

Labor Within Industry 4.0: Noah sees labor as a huge part of a connected digital factory, where cloud-based systems trigger actions on each other. His goal is to move manufacturing from fixed capacity toward on-demand operations.

q: What is Veryable and how does it work?

q: Why did Noah Labhart co-found Veryable?
a: The original idea came from his partner Mike Kinder, and Noah had supported manufacturing from an IT standpoint during eight years at Alcon Laboratories. q: How did Veryable solve the chicken-and-egg problem of a two-sided marketplace?

q: What was Veryable's biggest challenge to growth?

q: How did stimulus and unemployment payments affect Veryable?
a: Veryable saw short-lived pockets where there were not enough operators bidding on work, and workers returned when the money ran out. Noah said that "we've noticed that it's been directly correlated with stimulus" [10:19] payments or unemployment payments.

Test Before You Architect: EllisX built its MVP in about four weeks with Angular, Node and Firebase, deferring long-term architecture. Once traction came, the team spent a month or two rebuilding most of the code.

q: How did Richard Mensah choose his EllisX co-founder?

interview-on-product-journey

Workers First, Then Businesses: Veryable signed up roughly 200 to 300 workers before launch, then pitched businesses on that ready labor pool. Its first work opportunity, in February 2017, processed a $160 payment.

The Wrong Marketplace Hypothesis: The team expected workers to be harder to recruit than businesses. The opposite proved true: manufacturers needed education, relationships, face-to-face contact and a longer sales cycle.

Watching Users Find Friction: Early on, the team watched businesses post work, then shortened lengthy onboarding and job forms. Near misses got polish; features far off the mark were ditched, buried or changed.

Protecting the Core Product: About six months after launch, Veryable felt it had a core product the market wanted. Enhancements followed, such as next-day worker pay and favorites lists for businesses, without disrupting that core value.

Scaling Beyond the Monolith: The monolithic backend served well, but infrastructure forecasts showed about nine months before it would crack. The team is separating it into microservices using Docker and Kubernetes.

q: What is Veryable and what problem does it solve?
a: Veryable is a marketplace for on-demand labor in manufacturing and warehouse work, co-founded by Noah Labhart and CEO Mike Kinder. Labhart explained that manufacturers could not take advantage of costly new technology, saying "if they can't flex up and flex down their labor" [06:13].

q: How did Veryable solve the two-sided marketplace chicken-and-egg problem?
a: Labhart's team built the worker side first, promoting the app at warehouses, plants, schools and food trucks before approaching businesses. The initial 200 to 300 signups were modest, but Labhart noted they were enough "for really only needing a handful to start with one business" [09:29].

q: How did Veryable work toward product-market fit?
a: Labhart said there was no single moment, but about six months after launch the team felt it had a core product the market wanted. His approach was to "get the best thing you can get out quickly, and then ask, and then watch" [14:34].

q: How did Veryable scale its technology?
a: Labhart said Veryable built in the cloud on Amazon from the start, with a monolithic backend, and is now redesigning it around microservices. On scaling the original setup, he described "infrastructure scalability levers we've pulled until we essentially can't pull them anymore" [18:17].

q: How do you earn the trust of manufacturers when selling them new technology?
a: Labhart said Veryable skips the flashy sales pitch, focuses on operational problems and metrics, and tailors the message to executives, operations and HR. The message he described includes shared experience: "i've been in your seat this will really help you" [32:02].
